title: Far-field spatial coherence driven by lossy objects: first-principles approach unifying scattering of quantum light and thermal emission
abstract: Far-field spatial coherence dictates the interference properties of scattered light and thermal emission. Traditionally, these phenomena are treated through disjointed paradigms: classical scattering descriptions assume cold objects lacking quantum fluctuations, idealized quantum scattering schemes ignore dissipation, and semiclassical fluctuational electrodynamics relies on phenomenological noise currents, precluding the consistent treatment of incident quantum states. Here, we develop a first-principles framework based on the modified Langevin noise formalism to unify the scattering of quantum light and the intrinsic thermal emission of finite dissipative objects. We demonstrate that the outgoing far-field spatial coherence separates into an algebraic superposition of two geometry-driven mechanisms, coupled by the global unitarity of the radiation-matter dynamics. The first mechanism, elastic scattering, acts as a non-unitary spatial filter, mode-selectively attenuating and reshaping incident quantum correlations. The second mechanism, thermal emission, originates from localized material dissipation and projects the object's absorption profile into the far field, providing a quantum-vectorial derivation of the macroscopic van Cittert-Zernike theorem. Applying this framework across optical regimes, we determine operational bounds for lossy quantum photonics. Under chaotic thermal illumination, we analytically demonstrate thermal cloaking at equilibrium and show that a passive sink casts a structured thermal shadow geometrically identical to a primary emitter. Under coherent illumination, we derive a thermodynamic phase diagram bounding macroscopic phase correlations, demonstrating that subwavelength nanostructures undergo substantial coherence degradation compared to bulk objects. summary: The paper presents a first-principles quantum framework unifying how far-field spatial coherence is determined by both incident quantum light scattering and intrinsic thermal emission from dissipative objects. By using the Modified Langevin Noise Formalism, it shows that the outgoing coherence results from an algebraic sum of filtering (scattering) and projection (thermal emission) mechanisms. This has profound implications for designing lossy quantum optical components.
main_problem: To develop a first-principles framework that unifies the scattering of quantum light and intrinsic thermal emission from finite, dissipative objects to describe far-field spatial coherence.
main_result: The outgoing far-field spatial coherence separates into an algebraic superposition of two geometry-driven mechanisms: elastic scattering (a non-unitary filter) and thermal emission (deriving van Cittert-Zernike theorem).
method: The analysis employs the Modified Langevin Noise Formalism (MLNF) to calculate outgoing correlation dyadics, analyzing asymptotic limits for far-field correlations.
model_or_system: The system involves an arbitrary dispersive and absorbing magnetodielectric object interacting with incident quantum light fields. The theoretical foundation is built upon coupled radiation-matter operators within the MLNF framework.
key_observables: Far-field spatial coherence ($\mu^2_{	ext{out}}$), outgoing correlation dyadic ($	ext{C}_{	ext{out}}$), and thermal shadow structure.
important_parameters: Temperature ($T_{em}$), scattering cross-sections ($\sigma_{	ext{sca}}, \sigma_{	ext{abs}}$), and the dimensionless parameter $\Gamma$.
main_assumptions: The framework assumes rigorous description of material dissipation (Kirchhoff's law) and relies on statistical independence between incident radiation and object excitations in some derivations.
figures_summary: Figures schematically illustrate coherence generation across four thermodynamic limits: transparent, global equilibrium, cold vacuum, and cold scatterer, demonstrating the structured nature of the outgoing correlation dyadic.
paper_structure: The paper builds by first establishing the general input-output relationship using MLNF, then decomposing the resulting far-field correlation into scattering and thermal components, and finally analyzing specific physical limits (thermal/coherent illumination) to derive quantitative coherence bounds.
why_interesting: This work provides a unified quantum electrodynamic treatment of light propagation through realistic, lossy media, connecting fundamental principles like unitarity directly to macroscopic phenomena like the van Cittert-Zernike theorem and thermal cloaking.
